title: Can AI Mark Essays More Accurately Than Humans
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick examines a study in npj Science of Learning comparing large language models with human teachers on criterion-based marking of IELTS academic writing, and uses it to ask whether the practice of marking should be rethought rather than merely automated. The finding he foregrounds is a split verdict: the models were markedly more consistent than human graders but achieved only moderate absolute agreement with official examiners, an interrater figure of 0.61 with a wide confidence interval, even with carefully engineered prompts carrying full band descriptors. He treats that as telling precisely because IELTS writing is highly structured, so weak agreement in the easiest case casts doubt on readiness for more nuanced assessment. A second result he finds revealing is that more capable models did not mark better than ChatGPT 3.5, implying that domain-specific criteria matter more than general model sophistication, a point aimed at institutions choosing tools. Against the efficiency case, scale, no fatigue, no mood, he sets pattern-matching without comprehension, inherited dataset bias, over-reliance eroding critical evaluation, and teachers' sense that marking is how they come to know their students. His conclusion favours a human-in-the-loop arrangement, and he argues that even an imperfect AI has usefully exposed how poorly marking was already being justified.
points: The study's headline tension is that AI marking is more consistent than humans while remaining only moderately accurate against expert examiners, which makes consistency a weaker argument than it first appears.
Hendrick's sharpest inference is from context difficulty: if agreement is only moderate on highly rubric-structured IELTS writing, it should be worse on genuinely nuanced assessment.
The finding that ChatGPT 4.0 and Claude 3.0 Haiku performed no better than ChatGPT 3.5 implies procurement should prioritise criteria design over headline model capability.
The relational objection is given real weight: pupils often want evidence that effort was noticed more than an accurate judgement, which automation cannot supply.
His settled position is human-in-the-loop rather than replacement, citing Daisy Christodoulou, with AI absorbing routine marking so teachers can spend time on interaction.
quotes: Marking (or ‘grading’ in US money) is probably the most time-consuming and loathed aspects of a teacher’s weekly workload but emerging evidence suggests that things could be about to change.

The emergence of AI has intensified this debate, raising a fundamental question: if large language models can mark with greater consistency and objectivity than human teachers, should we be rethinking the entire practice of marking?

The study revealed that while AI models demonstrated superior consistency compared to human graders and showed moderate agreement with expert examiners, a crucial caveat emerged: even under optimal conditions with carefully engineered prompts incorporating detailed grading criteria, AI only achieved "moderate" absolute agreement with official IELTS examiners.
If AI can only achieve moderate agreement in such a well-defined context, it raises important questions about its readiness to handle more nuanced or complex assessment tasks.
Rather, this would seem to indicate that domain-specific knowledge and clear criteria matter more than the underlying sophistication of the AI model.
Very often, kids don’t care so much about how good a piece of work is, so much as they just want to know that you noticed their effort.
In the end I think the most promising path is the idea of merging human and AI capabilities.
